clue.text: Early gift for Peter and Gertrude

definitions.meaning: an old word for a first gift, a good-luck present given at the start of a new year or venture
the parents of the boy and his sister in Humperdinck's opera of the Grimm tale, so a gift for them is their son

explanation.surface: A christening present for a couple named Peter and Gertrude.
explanation.walkthrough: In Humperdinck's opera of the Grimm fairy tale the father is Peter and the mother Gertrude; 'for' links the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: the dated word for an inaugural good-luck gift, and the name of the fairy-tale boy whose operatic parents are Peter and Gertrude.

clue.text: Fondness shown by "Marguerite Duras" for John Hersey work

definitions.meaning: fondness here is love or a love affair, the French word used in English

definitions.text: shown by "Marguerite Duras" for John Hersey work
definitions.meaning: Hersey's book is called Hiroshima; Duras's screenplay title adds 'Mon' and this word to that city name

explanation.surface: A French novelist reveals her liking for an American journalist's reportage.
explanation.walkthrough: John Hersey's famous reportage is 'Hiroshima'; Marguerite Duras wrote the screenplay 'Hiroshima mon amour', so what she shows beyond Hersey's title ends in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Love is the plain sense of the French borrowing, and it is also the last word of the Duras film title built on Hersey's 'Hiroshima'.

clue.text: Stubborn defender of duodecimal system?

parts.note: a duodecimal system counts in twelves, read here as the twelve-tone method of composition, whose Austrian inventor championed it against all critics

explanation.surface: Someone who obstinately insists we should count in twelves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duodecimal system' suggests arithmetic or old money, but it means twelve-tone serial music, devised by the Austrian composer Arnold Schoenberg.
explanation.definitionFit: The composer invented the twelve-note serial method and defended it throughout his career against hostile audiences.

clue.text: Imperial survivor of Shakespearean bloodbath

parts.note: Titus Andronicus, Shakespeare's bloodiest play, ends with almost everyone dead except Titus's son, who is then proclaimed Roman emperor

explanation.surface: Someone from an empire who lived through a massacre in one of Shakespeare's plays.
explanation.walkthrough: The bloodbath is Titus Andronicus; Titus's one surviving son becomes emperor of Rome in the final scene.
explanation.definitionFit: In Titus Andronicus the hero's son outlives the carnage and is hailed as emperor, so he is the imperial survivor.

clue.text: Spotted trend in abstract painting

parts.note: a French name for a post-war abstract movement built on blobs and splashes of colour, from the French word for a stain or spot

explanation.surface: Noticing a new fashion in abstract art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' reads as 'noticed', but it describes the style itself: the French 'tache' means a spot or blot.
explanation.definitionFit: The movement's name comes from French 'tache', a blot, and its painters worked in dabs and blotches of paint.

clue.text: Van Gogh subjects in Chips with Everything?

definitions.text: Van Gogh subjects in Chips with Everything?

parts.words: Van Gogh subjects in Chips with Everything?
parts.note: Chips with Everything is an Arnold Wesker play; taken literally, people who eat chips with every meal are the peasants in Van Gogh's 1885 painting of a family at supper

explanation.surface: Asking whether Van Gogh's sitters turn up in Arnold Wesker's play.
explanation.walkthrough: Wesker's play title is read literally as a diet of fried potatoes, which suits the peasant family in Van Gogh's dark early painting.
explanation.definitionFit: Van Gogh's famous early painting shows a peasant family sharing a meal of potatoes by lamplight.

clue.text: He perceived the way of the world

definitions.text: He perceived the way of the world

parts.words: He perceived the way of the world
parts.note: the playwright wrote the Restoration comedy The Way of the World (1700), so he both saw and conceived that work

explanation.surface: A worldly-wise man who understood how life works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The way of the world' sounds like worldly wisdom, but it is the title of William Congreve's 1700 comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: William Congreve is the Restoration dramatist whose best-known comedy bears the title The Way of the World.

clue.text: Pseudonym of gaudy author

parts.note: J. I. M. Stewart wrote the Oxford novel The Gaudy under his own name and detective stories under a pen name, Michael ...

explanation.surface: The pen name of a writer of flashy books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gaudy' looks like 'garish', but The Gaudy (an Oxford college reunion feast) is a novel by J. I. M. Stewart, who wrote detective fiction as Michael Innes.
explanation.definitionFit: J. I. M. Stewart, author of The Gaudy, published his Appleby detective novels as Michael Innes, a pen name.

clue.text: Remind wit about Buchan work

indicators.note: about signals that the letters of the two words are moved around, turned about

explanation.surface: A jog to a joker's memory concerning something written by John Buchan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges REMIND WIT into the title of John Buchan's 1923 historical novel.
explanation.definitionFit: John Buchan's 1923 Jacobite adventure novel has this seasonal title.

clue.text: Dramatist's style makes Pooh's mess spotless

indicators.note: a mess of something is a jumble, so the letters of the bear's name are scrambled

parts.note: the possessive 's is kept as a letter S here
spotless means clean

explanation.surface: Winnie-the-Pooh's untidiness is turned into cleanliness by a classical playwright's manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mess' is the anagram signal working on the bear's name with its possessive S. The adjective refers to Sophocles, the Athenian tragedian, though the surface pictures a tidied nursery.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective for anything in the manner of Sophocles, the Athenian tragic playwright.

clue.text: Unadorned theme of Kenneth Clark

definitions.meaning: unadorned here means bare, wearing nothing
the art historian's 1956 study is subtitled A Study in Ideal Form and treats the undressed figure in art

explanation.surface: A plain, undecorated subject chosen by an art historian.
explanation.walkthrough: Kenneth Clark, the British art historian, wrote a classic book on the unclothed human body in Western art.
explanation.definitionFit: Unclothed means bare or unadorned, and Clark's famous book on the unclothed figure takes that word as its title.

clue.text: "If any be —'s legs, these are they: thou art very — indeed" (The Tempest)

definitions.text: "If any be —'s legs, these are they: thou art very — indeed" (The Tempest)

parts.words: "If any be —'s legs, these are they: thou art very — indeed" (The Tempest)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation: Stephano drags his drunken friend, the jester, out from under Caliban's cloak and greets him by name

explanation.surface: A line from The Tempest with a name blanked out twice.
explanation.walkthrough: In Act 2 scene 2 of The Tempest, the butler Stephano finds the jester hiding under Caliban's cloak and pulls him out by the legs.
explanation.definitionFit: The jester in The Tempest is the character Stephano names in this line as he pulls him from under Caliban's gaberdine.

clue.text: Critic takes ski run apart

indicators.note: taken apart, the letters of the two words are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: A reviewer pulls a ski slope to pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'apart' rearranges SKI RUN into the name of John Ruskin, the Victorian art critic.
explanation.definitionFit: John Ruskin was the leading Victorian art and social critic, author of Modern Painters.

clue.text: French writer's vocation lost in Arab bedsit

indicators.note: the letters are lost inside the run of the two words, concealed across the join

explanation.surface: A French author's calling vanishes in a rented room belonging to an Arab.
explanation.walkthrough: The French writer is the Abbé Prévost, author of Manon Lescaut, whose calling was the priesthood.
explanation.definitionFit: A French abbé is a cleric, the vocation of Prévost, who wrote as the Abbé Prévost.

clue.text: Something Beastly for Durrell's psychiatrist?

parts.note: Balthazar is the doctor in Durrell's Alexandria Quartet; Donleavy's novel The Beastly ... of Balthazar B gives the single blessing this asks for

explanation.surface: Something horrible awaits a psychiatrist in a Durrell novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A beatitude is a blessing; J. P. Donleavy's novel title pairs the plural with 'Beastly' and the name Balthazar, also a Durrell title.

clue.text: Recommend lawyer from West

definitions.meaning: to recommend a course is to argue for it, speak in its favour
Morris West's novel The Devil's ... takes its title from the Vatican official who argues against a canonisation, a lawyer in a sainthood case

explanation.surface: Suggesting a solicitor from the western part of the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West' looks like a compass point but is the Australian novelist Morris West, author of The Devil's Advocate (1959).
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to urge or back a cause; as a noun it is a pleader in court, the role in Morris West's title.

clue.text: Bardic gem produced by university

indicators.note: the letters are worked up into something new, produced as a different word

explanation.surface: A poet's jewel is turned out by a seat of learning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'produced' rearranges BARDIC GEM into the name of the English university.
explanation.definitionFit: Cambridge is one of England's two ancient universities, founded in the thirteenth century.

clue.text: Novelist seen to cavort with model in scam

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another, here the frolic and the car go inside the swindle

parts.note: a scam is a con
to cavort is to romp
T is the Model T, Ford's early car

explanation.surface: A writer is spotted frolicking with a fashion model during a swindle.
explanation.walkthrough: Richmal Crompton wrote the Just William books about an unruly English schoolboy.
explanation.definitionFit: Richmal Crompton was the English writer of the long-running Just William stories for children.

clue.text: Milne characters brought together by D. H. Lawrence

indicators.note: two separate names are brought together and joined end to end into one word

parts.note: the mother in Winnie-the-Pooh is Kanga
her baby in Winnie-the-Pooh is Roo

explanation.surface: Two of A. A. Milne's animals are united by a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Kanga and her baby Roo live in the Hundred Acre Wood; joined they name D. H. Lawrence's 1923 novel set in Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition is the novelist standing for his book: Lawrence's 1923 Australian novel has this marsupial title.

clue.text: Some further work of Max Beerbohm

definitions.meaning: Beerbohm followed his first book of essays with a second collection titled with this word (1899)

explanation.surface: Asking for additional pieces by the Edwardian humorist.
explanation.walkthrough: Max Beerbohm's first book was The Works of Max Beerbohm; the follow-up was simply called More.
explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: the word for an additional amount, and the title of Beerbohm's second essay collection.

clue.text: Sweetly inspirational poet associated with Sullivan operetta

definitions.text: Sweetly inspirational poet associated with Sullivan operetta

parts.words: Sweetly inspirational poet associated with Sullivan operetta
parts.note: the writer of uplifting greeting-card verse wrote as Patience ..., and Patience is also a Gilbert and Sullivan operetta

explanation.surface: A writer of syrupy uplifting verse with a link to a Savoy opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Patience Strong wrote sentimental inspirational verse for British newspapers; Patience is a Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera, so her surname is the poet that goes with it.
explanation.definitionFit: Patience Strong's verse was gently uplifting, and her first name matches Sullivan's operetta Patience.

clue.text: "I'm Irma": misleading statement by femme fatale in Hawthorne story

indicators.note: a misleading statement puts things the wrong way, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dangerous woman lies about her name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misleading' rearranges the letters of I'M IRMA. Miriam is the mysterious painter in Hawthorne's The Marble Faun.
explanation.definitionFit: The dark, alluring painter of Hawthorne's The Marble Faun draws Donatello into murder.

clue.text: Brand loyalty is expected of his admirers

definitions.text: Brand loyalty is expected of his admirers

parts.words: Brand loyalty is expected of his admirers
parts.note: brand loyalty is a marketing phrase, but Brand is a verse play by the Norwegian dramatist, so his fans should stand by it

explanation.surface: Fans of a product are expected to keep buying it.
explanation.walkthrough: Brand (1865) is a verse drama by Henrik Ibsen about an uncompromising priest.
explanation.definitionFit: Henrik Ibsen wrote the verse play Brand, so devotees of the Norwegian dramatist should be loyal to it.

clue.text: Fertility goddess seen in a store that's inexhaustible

indicators.note: the goddess is seen inside the phrase, running across its words

explanation.surface: A goddess of plenty appears in a shop whose stock never runs out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inexhaustible' points out that the hidden run does not use up all of 'that's'. Astoreth is the Phoenician goddess also spelt Ashtoreth or Astarte.
explanation.definitionFit: The Phoenician deity Astarte, called Ashtoreth in the Bible, was worshipped for fertility and sexual love.

clue.text: Northernmost destination of Longfellow

parts.note: the ancients' name for the farthest northern land, which Longfellow used for his collection Ultima ...

explanation.surface: The poet's journey ends at the most northerly point.
explanation.walkthrough: Longfellow's late collection is called Ultima Thule; Thule was the classical name for the farthest land in the north.
explanation.definitionFit: Classical geographers named the northernmost land Thule, and Longfellow made 'Ultima Thule' his book's title.

clue.text: Sprouts affectionately referred to by Bates

definitions.meaning: sprouts here are young shoots, as a noun
H. E. Bates's novel is The Darling ... of May, where they are called darling

explanation.surface: Brussels sprouts get a fond mention from a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: H. E. Bates took his title The Darling Buds of May from Shakespeare's Sonnet 18; 'darling' is the affection.
explanation.definitionFit: Young shoots on a plant are its first growth, and Bates called them darling in his novel's title.

clue.text: Poe creature which may have bitten some B. Traven protagonists

definitions.text: Poe creature which may have bitten some B. Traven protagonists

parts.words: Poe creature which may have bitten some B. Traven protagonists
parts.note: Poe's story about a beetle and buried treasure; to be bitten by this creature is to catch treasure fever, as the prospectors of The Treasure of the Sierra Madre do

explanation.surface: An insect from Poe that might have stung characters in a Traven novel.
explanation.walkthrough: B. Traven wrote The Treasure of the Sierra Madre, whose prospectors are consumed by greed; being bitten by this insect is a phrase for gold fever.
explanation.definitionFit: Poe's 1843 tale centres on a gleaming scarab and a treasure hunt, and its insect stands for the craving for riches.

clue.text: He went to school at Linbury Court in 1950

definitions.text: He went to school at Linbury Court in 1950

parts.words: He went to school at Linbury Court in 1950
parts.note: Anthony Buckeridge's schoolboy hero first appears in a 1950 book about arriving at Linbury Court prep school

explanation.surface: A boy who started at a particular boarding school in 1950.
explanation.walkthrough: Linbury Court is the fictional prep school in Anthony Buckeridge's children's books, the first published in 1950.
explanation.definitionFit: The schoolboy hero of Buckeridge's series attends Linbury Court, first appearing in a 1950 book about going to school.

clue.text: Reportedly grim sibling of!

parts.note: said aloud, grim is Grimm, the brothers' fairy tale; the girl is the sister of 1 across, whose number the page prints as an exclamation mark

explanation.surface: A gloomy-sounding brother or sister.
explanation.walkthrough: The '!' is the number 1, pointing to 1 across, misread in the printed text; 'reportedly grim' sounds like Grimm.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Brothers Grimm tale the girl lost in the woods is the sister of the boy at 1 across.
